claim: Synaptic vesicles (SVs) are specialized organelles that store and secrete non-peptide neurotransmitters at synapses.
source: Synaptic vesicles (SVs) are the specialized organelles that store and secrete non-peptide neurotransmitters at synapses.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about synaptic vesicle function.

claim: Following exocytosis, synaptic vesicle membranes are rapidly recaptured by endocytosis and recycled for the generation of new fusion-competent SVs.
source: Following exocytosis, their membranes are rapidly recaptured by endocytosis and recycled for the generation of new fusion-competent SVs (Ceccarelli et al., 1973; Heuser and Reese, 1973; Betz and Bewick, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Clathrin-mediated endocytosis (CME) plays a key role in synaptic vesicle endocytic traffic.
source: Strong evidence indicates that clathrin-mediated endocytosis (CME) plays a key role in this endocytic traffic (Heuser and Reese, 1973; Maycox et al., 1992; Granseth et al., 2006; Heerssen et al., 2008; Kasprowicz et al., 2008; Saheki and De Camilli, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Endocytic vesicles generated by CME have a small homogenous size, in the same range of SVs.
source: Endocytic vesicles generated by CME have a small homogenous size, in the same range of SVs (Shupliakov et al., 1997; Raimondi et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Clathrin-coated vesicles may mature directly into SVs without transiting through an endosomal station.
source: While it had been originally hypothesized that such vesicles transit through an endosomal station (Heuser and Reese, 1973), subsequent studies have suggested that they may mature directly into SVs, a possibility consistent with their size (Takei et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: CME does not account for all SV recycling.
source: However, CME does not account for all SV recycling and the mechanisms of alternative pathways have been the object of intense debate.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of CME in SV recycling, drawing on established knowledge.

claim: Kiss-and-run is a proposed alternative recycling mechanism whereby SVs fuse only very transiently with the plasma membrane without collapsing into it.
source: One proposed alternative recycling mechanism is so-called 'kiss-and-run', a process whereby SVs fuse only very transiently with the plasma membrane without collapsing into it, so that the SVs reform directly by the immediate closure of the fusion pore (Fesce et al., 1994; Alabi and Tsien, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Bulk endocytosis is a high capacity pathway of plasma membrane internalization involving patches of membrane larger than the membrane of individual SVs.
source: Yet another mechanism is bulk endocytosis, a high capacity pathway of plasma membrane internalization involving patches of membrane larger than the membrane of individual SVs.
evidence: This is a definition of bulk endocytosis based on established knowledge.

claim: Bulk endocytosis predominates under intense neuronal activity.
source: This mechanism predominates under intense neuronal activity (Miller and Heuser, 1984; Holt et al., 2003; Wu and Wu, 2007; Hayashi et al., 2008; Cousin, 2009; Wenzel et al., 2012; Kittelmann et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Bulk endosomes eventually disappear as new SVs appear, suggesting a precursor-product relationship.
source: Endocytic intermediates generated by bulk endocytosis, henceforth defined as 'bulk' endosomes, eventually disappear as new SVs appear, suggesting a precursor-product relationship and possibly a direct formation of SVs from bulk endosomes (Heuser and Reese, 1973).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research and involves inference about the relationship between bulk endosomes and SVs.

claim: Mutations expected to result in loss or strong defect of the function of clathrin or AP-2 in C. elegans were shown not to abolish synaptic function.
source: Mutations expected to result in loss or strong defect of the function of clathrin or of its endocytic adaptor AP-2 were shown not to abolish synaptic function (Gu et al., 2008, 2013; Sato et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Studies of worm synapses expressing channelrhodopsin and subjected to a very brief photostimulus revealed an ultrafast endocytic reaction mediated by uncoated invaginations larger than SVs.
source: Additionally, studies of worm synapses expressing channelrhodopsin and subjected to a very brief photostimulus revealed an ultrafast endocytic reaction mediated by uncoated invaginations larger than SVs (Watanabe et al., 2013a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: An ultrafast endocytic reaction mediated by large uncoated invaginations in response to a single optogenetic stimulus was observed at synapses of mouse hippocampal neurons in primary culture.
source: More recently, similar results – an ultrafast endocytic reaction mediated by large uncoated invaginations in response to a single optogenetic stimulus – were observed at synapses of mouse hippocampal neurons in primary culture (Watanabe et al., 2013b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The molecular mechanisms underlying bulk endocytosis remain poorly understood.
source: Both the molecular mechanisms underlying bulk endocytosis and those through which SVs are generated from bulk endosomes remain poorly understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The mechanisms through which SVs are generated from bulk endosomes remain poorly understood.
source: Both the molecular mechanisms underlying bulk endocytosis and those through which SVs are generated from bulk endosomes remain poorly understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Dynamin is a GTPase known to mediate endocytic membrane fission in multiple contexts including endocytic fission at neuronal synapses.
source: Thus, several studies of bulk endocytosis have addressed the potential involvement of dynamin, a GTPase known to mediate endocytic membrane fission in multiple contexts including, most prominently, endocytic fission at neuronal synapses (Koenig and Ikeda, 1989; Ramaswami et al., 1994; Ferguson and De Camilli, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Some studies have supported a role for dynamin 1 in bulk endocytosis.
source: A role for dynamin, and more specifically for dynamin 1 has been supported by some studies (Clayton et al., 2009, 2010; Xue et al., 2011; Nguyen et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Dynamin 1 is constitutively phosphorylated in resting nerve terminals and its Ca2+ triggered dephosphorylation upon synaptic stimulation results in its binding to syndapin/pacsin.
source: Interestingly, dynamin 1 is constitutively phosphorylated in resting nerve terminals and its Ca2+ triggered dephosphorylation upon synaptic stimulation results in its binding to the F-BAR domain containing protein syndapin/pacsin (Anggono et al., 2006; Clayton et al., 2009; Koch et al., 2011), which has also been implicated in bulk endocytosis (Andersson et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Syndapin/pacsin has been implicated in bulk endocytosis.
source: Interestingly, dynamin 1 is constitutively phosphorylated in resting nerve terminals and its Ca2+ triggered dephosphorylation upon synaptic stimulation results in its binding to the F-BAR domain containing protein syndapin/pacsin (Anggono et al., 2006; Clayton et al., 2009; Koch et al., 2011), which has also been implicated in bulk endocytosis (Andersson et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Studies of dynamin 1 knock-out neurons have indicated the occurrence of robust bulk endocytosis even in the absence of dynamin 1.
source: However, studies of dynamin 1 knock-out (KO) neurons have indicated the occurrence of robust bulk endocytosis even in the absence of dynamin 1 (Hayashi et al., 2008), in spite of a strong impairment of CME (Ferguson et al., 2007; Lou et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: CME is strongly impaired in dynamin 1 knock-out neurons.
source: However, studies of dynamin 1 knock-out (KO) neurons have indicated the occurrence of robust bulk endocytosis even in the absence of dynamin 1 (Hayashi et al., 2008), in spite of a strong impairment of CME (Ferguson et al., 2007; Lou et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Dynamin 3 may substitute for dynamin 1 in dynamin 1 knock-out neurons.
source: It remains possible that other dynamins, dynamin 3 in particular, which is the other predominantly neuronal dynamin, may substitute for dynamin 1 in these neurons (Ferguson et al., 2007; Raimondi et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research and involves speculation about the role of dynamin 3.

claim: Drugs (dyngo-4a and dynasore) that impair dynamin activity were reported to block bulk endocytosis.
source: Drugs (dyngo-4a and dynasore) that impair dynamin activity were reported to block bulk endocytosis (Nguyen et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Dynamin inhibitor drugs can robustly affect plasma membrane dynamics by dynamin-independent mechanisms.
source: However, the interpretation of such results is questioned by the more recent demonstration that these drugs can robustly affect plasma membrane dynamics by dynamin-independent mechanisms (Park et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: It was proposed that conversion of bulk endosomes to SVs occurs via the same clathrin-mediated budding reaction that drives clathrin-mediated budding from the plasma membrane.
source: Based on a study of 'broken' synaptosomes it was proposed that such a conversion occurs via the same clathrin-mediated budding reaction that drives clathrin-mediated budding from the plasma membrane (Takei et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: In the study by Takei et al. (1996), bulk endosomes were exposed to conditions that can induce ectopic production of PI(4,5)P2.
source: However, in that study bulk endosomes were exposed to conditions that can induce ectopic production of PI(4,5)P2 (incubation with ATP and GTP or GTPγS) (Seaman et al., 1993; Takei et al., 1996; Krauss et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Assembly of endocytic coats critically requires PI(4,5)P2 in the membrane from which they originate.
source: Subsequent evidence that assembly of endocytic coats critically requires PI(4,5)P2 in the membrane from which they originate (Cremona et al., 1999; Höning et al., 2005; Zoncu et al., 2007; Idevall-Hagren et al., 2012) challenged these results as PI(4,5)P2, which is selectively concentrated at the plasma membrane, is generally rapidly depleted from endocytic membranes and is thus not expected to be concentrated on bulk endosomes (Cremona et al., 1999; Chang-Ileto et al., 2011; Milosevic et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: PI(4,5)P2 is selectively concentrated at the plasma membrane and is generally rapidly depleted from endocytic membranes.
source: Subsequent evidence that assembly of endocytic coats critically requires PI(4,5)P2 in the membrane from which they originate (Cremona et al., 1999; Höning et al., 2005; Zoncu et al., 2007; Idevall-Hagren et al., 2012) challenged these results as PI(4,5)P2, which is selectively concentrated at the plasma membrane, is generally rapidly depleted from endocytic membranes and is thus not expected to be concentrated on bulk endosomes (Cremona et al., 1999; Chang-Ileto et al., 2011; Milosevic et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: PI(4,5)P2 is not expected to be concentrated on bulk endosomes.
source: Subsequent evidence that assembly of endocytic coats critically requires PI(4,5)P2 in the membrane from which they originate (Cremona et al., 1999; Höning et al., 2005; Zoncu et al., 2007; Idevall-Hagren et al., 2012) challenged these results as PI(4,5)P2, which is selectively concentrated at the plasma membrane, is generally rapidly depleted from endocytic membranes and is thus not expected to be concentrated on bulk endosomes (Cremona et al., 1999; Chang-Ileto et al., 2011; Milosevic et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research and involves inference about PI(4,5)P2 localization.

claim: The rapid, bulk endocytic recapture of SV membranes induced by a strong stimulus is not impaired at synapses lacking both dynamin 1 and dynamin 3.
source: We demonstrate that the rapid, bulk endocytic recapture of SV membranes induced by a strong stimulus, either KCl or high frequency stimulation, is not impaired at synapses lacking both of the two predominant neuronal dynamins, dynamin 1 and dynamin 3, that is synapses where CME is severely perturbed (Ferguson et al., 2007; Raimondi et al., 2011; Ferguson and De Camilli, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study and citations to prior research.

claim: CME is severely perturbed at synapses lacking both dynamin 1 and dynamin 3.
source: We demonstrate that the rapid, bulk endocytic recapture of SV membranes induced by a strong stimulus, either KCl or high frequency stimulation, is not impaired at synapses lacking both of the two predominant neuronal dynamins, dynamin 1 and dynamin 3, that is synapses where CME is severely perturbed (Ferguson et al., 2007; Raimondi et al., 2011; Ferguson and De Camilli, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Conversion of bulk endosomes into new SVs occurs in dynamin 1/3 double KO synapses, although less efficiently than in wild-type synapses.
source: Conversion of bulk endosomes into new SVs does occur in these synapses, although less efficiently than in wild-type (WT) synapses.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: The partial impairment of conversion of bulk endosomes to SVs is not further aggravated by the additional knock-down of clathrin.
source: The partial impairment of this conversion is not further aggravated by the additional knock-down (KD) of clathrin, indicating the clathrin-independence of this process.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: There exists a pathway of SV reformation that predominates after strong stimulation and does not require clathrin mediated budding or dynamin 1 and 3.
source: These observations provide evidence for a pathway of SV reformation that predominates after strong stimulation and does not require clathrin mediated budding or dynamin 1 and 3.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study and involves inference about the existence of an alternative pathway.

claim: In WT synapses, the number of SVs per synapse was reduced to about 20% of the starting value at the end of 90 s stimulation with 90 mM KCl.
source: Analysis of samples fixed at the end of the 90 s stimulation revealed that in WT synapses the number of SVs per synapse (number per μm2 of synapse cross-section) was reduced to about 20% of the starting value (Figures 1A and 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the figures.

claim: The reduction in SV number in WT synapses after stimulation was accompanied by a massive appearance of endocytic vacuoles much larger than SVs (bulk endosomes).
source: Such reduction was accompanied by a massive appearance of endocytic vacuoles much larger than SVs, that is bulk endosomes (as defined by a diameter greater than 80 nm), nearly all of which were positive for CTX-HRP, as assessed by HRP cytochemistry (Figures 1A and 2A,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the figures.

claim: Bulk endosomes are defined as having a diameter greater than 80 nm.
source: Such reduction was accompanied by a massive appearance of endocytic vacuoles much larger than SVs, that is bulk endosomes (as defined by a diameter greater than 80 nm), nearly all of which were positive for CTX-HRP, as assessed by HRP cytochemistry (Figures 1A and 2A,C).
evidence: This is a definition provided by the authors.

claim: Nearly all bulk endosomes formed after stimulation were positive for CTX-HRP.
source: Such reduction was accompanied by a massive appearance of endocytic vacuoles much larger than SVs, that is bulk endosomes (as defined by a diameter greater than 80 nm), nearly all of which were positive for CTX-HRP, as assessed by HRP cytochemistry (Figures 1A and 2A,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the figures.

claim: Similar changes in SV number and bulk endosome formation were observed in Dyn3 KO synapses as in WT synapses.
source: Similar changes were observed in Dyn3 KO synapses (Figure 1A, Figure 2B,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the figures.

claim: In both Dyn1 KO synapses and Dyn1/3 DKO synapses, SVs were nearly completely depleted at the end of the stimulus.
source: In contrast, in both Dyn1 KO synapses and Dyn1/3 DKO synapses, SVs were nearly completely depleted at the end of the stimulus (Figures 1A, 2A,B), indicating that SV reformation is blocked in these genotypes during stimulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the figures.

claim: SV reformation is blocked in Dyn1 KO and Dyn1/3 DKO genotypes during stimulation.
source: In contrast, in both Dyn1 KO synapses and Dyn1/3 DKO synapses, SVs were nearly completely depleted at the end of the stimulus (Figures 1A, 2A,B), indicating that SV reformation is blocked in these genotypes during stimulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the figures and involves inference about SV reformation.

claim: Dyn1 KO and Dyn1/3 DKO synapses had a greater number of large endocytic intermediates (diameter >80 nm) relative to WT and Dyn3 KO synapses.
source: This difference was accompanied by a greater number of large endocytic intermediates (diameter >80 nm) in these genotypes, relative to WT and to Dyn3 KO synapses (Figures 1A and 2B,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the figures.

claim: Bulk endocytosis is not impaired, and perhaps is even enhanced, in the absence of both Dyn1 and Dyn3.
source: Importantly, these findings demonstrate that bulk endocytosis is not impaired, and perhaps is even enhanced, in the absence of both Dyn1 and Dyn3.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study and involves inference about the role of dynamins.

claim: A very robust recovery of SV number was already observed after 10 min of recovery in WT and Dyn3 KO synapses.
source: Following the stimulus, a very robust recovery of SV number was already observed after 10 min of recovery in WT and Dyn3 KO synapses (Figures 1A and 2A,B), with a corresponding decrease of HRP reaction product-positive large vacuoles (Figure 2C,D), and this recovery continued thereafter (Figures 1A, 2A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the figures.

claim: Recovery of SV number in WT and Dyn3 KO synapses was accompanied by a corresponding decrease of HRP reaction product-positive large vacuoles.
source: Following the stimulus, a very robust recovery of SV number was already observed after 10 min of recovery in WT and Dyn3 KO synapses (Figures 1A and 2A,B), with a corresponding decrease of HRP reaction product-positive large vacuoles (Figure 2C,D), and this recovery continued thereafter (Figures 1A, 2A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the figures.

claim: Recovery (both an increase in SV number and a decrease in larger endocytic intermediates) was also observed in Dyn1 KO and Dyn1/3 DKO synapses, although both SV reformation and endocytic vacuole clearance were delayed relative to littermate controls.
source: Recovery (both an increase in SV number and a decrease in larger endocytic intermediates) was also observed in Dyn1 KO and Dyn1/3 DKO synapses, although both SV reformation and endocytic vacuole clearance were delayed relative to littermate controls (WT and Dyn3 KO respectively; Figure 2A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the figures.

claim: The overall similar results for WT and Dyn3 KO cultures and for Dyn1 KO and Dyn1/3 DKO cultures confirm the predominant role of dynamin 1 in SV recycling.
source: Note that the overall similar results for WT and Dyn3 KO cultures and for Dyn1 KO and Dyn1/3 DKO cultures, confirm previously reported evidence for the predominant role of dynamin 1 in SV recycling.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study and involves inference about the role of dynamin 1.

claim: In all samples exposed to CTX-HRP during stimulation and recovery, the majority of newly reformed SVs were labeled.
source: In all samples exposed to this experimental protocol, the majority of newly reformed SVs were labeled (dark portions of each bar in Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the figures.

claim: At the end of the 90 s stimulation, the majority of the remaining SVs in WT and Dyn3 KO synapses were labeled, indicating that they had formed by endocytic recycling during the stimulus.
source: Interestingly, even at the end of the 90 s stimulation, the majority of the remaining SVs in WT and Dyn3 KO synapses were labeled, indicating that they had formed by endocytic recycling during the stimulus (Figure 1, Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the figures and involves inference about SV formation.

claim: In all four genotypes the high K+ stimulus induces the exocytosis of all SVs.
source: As SVs had been nearly depleted in Dyn1 KO and Dyn1/3 DKO synapses at this time point (Figure 2A,B), one can conclude that in all four genotypes the high K+ stimulus induces the exocytosis of all SVs, but that only at synapses containing dynamin 1 SV reformation occur during the stimulus, thus partially counteracting the loss of SVs (see also Ferguson et al., 2007; Raimondi et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the figures and involves inference about exocytosis.

claim: Only at synapses containing dynamin 1 does SV reformation occur during the stimulus, thus partially counteracting the loss of SVs.
source: As SVs had been nearly depleted in Dyn1 KO and Dyn1/3 DKO synapses at this time point (Figure 2A,B), one can conclude that in all four genotypes the high K+ stimulus induces the exocytosis of all SVs, but that only at synapses containing dynamin 1 SV reformation occur during the stimulus, thus partially counteracting the loss of SVs (see also Ferguson et al., 2007; Raimondi et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the figures, citations to prior research, and involves inference about SV reformation.

claim: When CTX-HRP was added only during the recovery phase, only very few large vacuoles were HRP labeled, indicating that bulk endocytosis occurs nearly exclusively during the high K+ stimulation.
source: To discriminate between these possibilities, cultures of all four genotypes were exposed to CTX-HRP only during the recovery phase, following a 90 s stimulus, and then analyzed at the 10 and 30 min time points (Figure 1B, Figure 2E–H). In these samples, only very few large vacuoles were HRP labeled (Figure 2G,H), indicating that bulk endocytosis occurs nearly exclusively during the high K+ stimulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the figures and involves inference about the timing of bulk endocytosis.

claim: The fraction of CTX-HRP labeled newly reformed SVs, relative to all SVs, was much lower when CTX-HRP was added only after the stimulus compared to when it was added during and after the stimulus.
source: If the conversion of bulk endosomes to SVs during stimulation requires their prior fusion with the plasma membrane, using this protocol the majority of newly reformed SVs should be labeled. This was not the case, as the fraction of CTX-HRP labeled newly reformed SVs, relative to all SVs, was much lower than in samples incubated with CTX-HRP both during and after the stimulus (compare the solid to empty portions of the bars in Figure 2E,F and in Figure 2A,B, respectively, see also Figure 2I).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the figures.

claim: During recovery a large pool of SVs reforms directly from the bulk endosomes that were generated during the stimulus.
source: These findings imply that during recovery a large pool of SVs reforms directly from the bulk endosomes that were generated during the stimulus.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study and involves inference about SV reformation.

claim: The number of CTX-HRP positive SVs generated during post-stimulus endocytosis was only modestly decreased in Dyn1 KO and Dyn1/3 DKO synapses relative to their controls.
source: Note that the number of CTX-HRP positive SVs, that is SVs generated during post-stimulus endocytosis, was only modestly decreased in Dyn1 KO and Dyn1/3 DKO synapses relative to their controls (Figure 2E,F), suggesting that either clathrin/dynamin-dependent SV endocytosis is not involved in their formation or that dynamin/clathrin-mediated endocytosis occurring during the recovery can be sustained by dynamin 2 even though the levels of this dynamin isoform in neurons are very low compared to either dynamin 1 or 3 (Ferguson et al., 2007; Raimondi et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the figures and involves speculation about the mechanisms of SV formation.

claim: SV reformation occurs even in the absence of Dyn1 and Dyn3, but this process is substantially delayed.
source: Our conclusions from these comparisons are as follows: (1) SV reformation occurs even in the absence of Dyn1 and Dyn3, but this process is substantially delayed as shown by the missing portion of the pie;
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study and involves inference from the pie chart analysis.

claim: No SV reformation occurs during the stimulus in the absence of Dyn1 or both Dyn1 and 3, leading to complete SV depletion.
source: (2) No SV reformation occurs during the stimulus in the absence of Dyn1 or both Dyn1 and 3 (solid black sections), leading to complete SV depletion;
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study and involves inference from the pie chart analysis.

claim: Reformation of SVs by endocytosis that occurs after the interruption of the stimulus is surprisingly similar in all genotypes.
source: (3) Reformation of SVs by endocytosis that occurs after the interruption of the stimulus is surprisingly similar in all genotypes (red stripes sector);
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study and involves inference from the pie chart analysis.

claim: Most of the delay in recovery in dynamin KO neurons is due to a delay in the conversion from bulk endosomes to SVs.
source: (4) Most of the delay in recovery in dynamin KO neurons is due to a delay in the conversion from bulk endosomes to SVs (black stripes).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study and involves inference from the pie chart analysis.

claim: Fluid phase HRP labels endocytic vesicles less efficiently than CTX-HRP.
source: While this probe labels endocytic vesicles less efficiently than CTX-HRP, as it is not bound to, and therefore concentrated at, membranes, it can be rapidly washed away from the cell surface, and thus can be used to better analyze endocytosis in a specific time window.
evidence: This is a statement about the properties of fluid phase HRP based on established knowledge.

claim: Fluid phase HRP can be rapidly washed away from the cell surface.
source: While this probe labels endocytic vesicles less efficiently than CTX-HRP, as it is not bound to, and therefore concentrated at, membranes, it can be rapidly washed away from the cell surface, and thus can be used to better analyze endocytosis in a specific time window.
evidence: This is a statement about the properties of fluid phase HRP based on established knowledge.

claim: There was a further increase of HRP-labeled SVs during the recovery in the HRP-free medium, and a corresponding decrease of larger vacuoles, indicating a contribution of HRP reaction product-positive vacuoles formed during the stimulus to SV reformation.
source: Importantly, there was a further increase of HRP-labeled SVs during the recovery in the HRP-free medium, and a corresponding decrease of larger vacuoles, indicating a contribution of HRP reaction product-positive vacuoles formed during the stimulus to SV reformation (Figures 3 and 4A,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the figures and involves inference about SV reformation.

claim: Neither Dyn1 nor Dyn3 is required for bulk endocytosis.
source: Collectively, these experiments demonstrate that neither Dyn1 nor Dyn3 is required for bulk endocytosis and that their absence delays, but does not abolish, SV reformation from internal membranes.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: The absence of Dyn1 and Dyn3 delays, but does not abolish, SV reformation from internal membranes.
source: Collectively, these experiments demonstrate that neither Dyn1 nor Dyn3 is required for bulk endocytosis and that their absence delays, but does not abolish, SV reformation from internal membranes.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: Vesicles labeled by the endocytic tracer are competent for a new cycle of stimulated secretion.
source: It was important to show that vesicles labeled by the endocytic tracer are indeed bona fide SVs, that is that they are competent for a new cycle of stimulated secretion. To address this issue, Dyn1/3 DKO cultures, and Dyn3 KO cultures as controls, were exposed to high K+ stimulation in the presence of soluble HRP, then washed and further incubated for 30 min in resting medium in the absence of HRP, exposed to a second high K+ stimulus, and finally rested again for 30 min, always in the absence of HRP. As shown by EM analysis at the end of each period (Figure 5), the second stimulus was as effective as the first in inducing exocytosis of both labeled and unlabeled SVs.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the figures.

claim: The second stimulus was as effective as the first in inducing exocytosis of both labeled and unlabeled SVs.
source: As shown by EM analysis at the end of each period (Figure 5), the second stimulus was as effective as the first in inducing exocytosis of both labeled and unlabeled SVs.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the figures.

claim: 80 Hz electrical stimulation yielded results very similar to those produced by high K+ stimulation.
source: 80 Hz electrical stimulation yielded results very similar to those produced by high K+ stimulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: A robust reduction in SV number was observed immediately after 80 Hz electrical stimulation, and this effect was stronger at Dyn1/3 DKO synapses.
source: A robust reduction in SV number was observed immediately after stimulation, and this effect was stronger at Dyn1/3 DKO synapses.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: When CTX-HRP labeling was present during 80 Hz stimulation, some labeled SVs were observed at the end of the stimulus, but only in the control (Dyn3 KO) cultures.
source: Even in this case, when CTX-HRP labeling was present during stimulation, some labeled SVs were observed at the end of the stimulus, but only in the control (Dyn3 KO) cultures (Figure 6A,B, and black sector in the pie chart of Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the figures.

claim: The strongest defects observed at Dyn1/3 DKO synapses relative to controls after 80 Hz stimulation concern the reformation of SVs during the stimulus and the recovery of SVs from CTX-HRP labeled bulk endosomes generated during the stimulus.
source: As the pie chart of Figure 6C shows (labeling of the sectors is the same as in Figure 2I), the strongest defects observed at Dyn1/3 DKO synapses relative to controls concern the reformation of SVs during the stimulus (black sector) and the recovery of SVs from CTX-HRP labeled bulk endosomes generated during the stimulus (sector with black stripes).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the figures and involves inference from the pie chart analysis.

claim: CCPs were nearly absent before stimulation in synapses of all genotypes, including Dyn1 KO and Dyn1/3 DKO synapses.
source: CCPs were nearly absent before stimulation in synapses of all genotypes, including Dyn1 KO and Dyn1/3 DKO synapses (Figure 7A–D), as spontaneous network activity prior to the stimulation had been silenced by an overnight treatment with TTX.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the figures.

claim: Upon stimulation, CCP number increased only slightly in WT and Dyn3 KO synapses, but more strongly in Dyn1 KO and Dyn1/3 DKO synapses.
source: Upon stimulation, CCP number increased only slightly in WT and Dyn3 KO synapses, but more strongly in Dyn1 KO and Dyn1/3 DKO synapses (Figure 7A–D), where numerous CCPs located deep inside nerve terminals were observed.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the figures.

claim: Numerous CCPs located deep inside nerve terminals were observed in Dyn1 KO and Dyn1/3 DKO synapses.
source: Upon stimulation, CCP number increased only slightly in WT and Dyn3 KO synapses, but more strongly in Dyn1 KO and Dyn1/3 DKO synapses (Figure 7A–D), where numerous CCPs located deep inside nerve terminals were observed.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the figures.

claim: CCPs deep inside nerve terminals were accessible to CTX-HRP added during recovery, as reflected by the presence of HRP reaction product in their core.
source: Such CCPs were accessible to CTX-HRP added during recovery, as reflected by the presence of HRP reaction product in their core (Figure 7A,B,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the figures.

claim: In samples incubated with fluid-phase HRP during the 90 s stimulation and then immediately washed, CCPs were observed only on HRP reaction product-negative membranes.
source: However, in these samples, CCPs were observed only on HRP reaction product-negative membranes (Figure 7B,D,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the figures.

claim: CCP formation in response to high K+ stimulation predominantly occurs on the plasma membrane and not on endocytic intermediates formed by bulk endocytosis.
source: These results indicate that CCP formation in response to high K+ stimulation predominantly occurs on the plasma membrane and not on endocytic intermediates formed by bulk endocytosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study and involves inference about CCP localization.

claim: EM tomography confirmed that CCPs present deep inside terminals were connected to the plasma membrane.
source: EM tomography further confirmed that CCPs present deep inside terminals were connected to the plasma membrane.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: No CCPs were observed on bulk endosomes in either WT or Dyn1 KO synapses in tomographic reconstructions.
source: No CCPs (green) were observed on bulk endosomes (yellow, identified by an HRP reaction product-positive core and anatomical separation from the plasma membrane) in either WT or Dyn1 KO.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the figures.

claim: The overall appearance and distribution of HRP reaction product-positive vacuoles was similar in WT and Dyn1 KO genotypes: irregular cisternae, which in some cases had tubulated portions.
source: Furthermore, the overall appearance and distribution of HRP reaction product-positive vacuoles (yellow) was similar in the two genotypes: irregular cisternae, which in some cases had tubulated portions. (Figure 8A,C and selected examples in Figure 8E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the figures.

claim: CCPs in Dyn1 KO synapses were selectively localized on deep, narrow invaginations of the plasma membrane.
source: CCPs were frequently found in Dyn1 KO synapses and massively abundant at a subset of Dyn1 KO synapses, but in these synapses they were selectively localized on deep, narrow invaginations of the plasma membrane (Figure 8D) (a connection between one such invagination and the plasma membrane is shown in the inset of Figure 8D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the figures.

claim: High pressure freezing/freeze-substitution revealed a more compact texture of the neuronal cytoplasm and a different view of endocytic structures induced by stimulation relative to conventionally fixed material.
source: EM analysis of these preparations revealed a more compact texture of the neuronal cytoplasm and a different view of endocytic structures induced by stimulation relative to conventionally fixed material.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: The great majority of bulk endosomes in high-pressure frozen samples had smoother rounded or oval-shaped profiles.
source: The great majority of bulk endosomes, which had an electron-lucent lumen, had smoother rounded or oval-shaped profiles (Figure 9A, see also tomographic reconstructions at 3 min recovery in Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the figures.

claim: Coated buds were only occasionally observed on vacuolar structures in high-pressure frozen samples.
source: Only occasionally (WT: 8 of 275; Dyn1 KO: 15 of 249; Dyn3 KO: 8 of 235; Dyn1/3 DKO: 32 of 258 synapses) were coated buds observed on vacuolar structures (Figure 9B) and, with only one exception, when the entire profile of these structures was re-constructed within tomograms, they were found to be continuous with the plasma membrane (Figure 9B, field B4 and Figure 9C, field C4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the figures.

claim: With only one exception, when the entire profile of vacuolar structures with coated buds was reconstructed within tomograms, they were found to be continuous with the plasma membrane.
source: Only occasionally (WT: 8 of 275; Dyn1 KO: 15 of 249; Dyn3 KO: 8 of 235; Dyn1/3 DKO: 32 of 258 synapses) were coated buds observed on vacuolar structures (Figure 9B) and, with only one exception, when the entire profile of these structures was re-constructed within tomograms, they were found to be continuous with the plasma membrane (Figure 9B, field B4 and Figure 9C, field C4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the figures.

claim: CCP 'trees' were only observed in recovered Dyn 1/3 DKO synapses.
source: As expected, CCP 'trees' were only observed in recovered Dyn 1/3 DKO synapses (Figure 9C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the figures.

claim: Tubulated, beaded extensions of some bulk endosomes were visible in high-pressure frozen preparations, suggesting the potential occurrence of new SVs by progressive fragmentation.
source: Tubulated, beaded extensions of some bulk endosomes were also visible in these preparations (Figure 9—figure supplement 1, Figure 9D), suggesting the potential occurrence of new SVs by progressive fragmentation.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the figures and involves speculation about SV formation.

claim: A morphometric analysis of thin sections from high-pressure frozen and freeze-substituted specimens revealed a narrow range of SV diameters that peaked at 30 nm at resting synapses.
source: In fact, a morphometric analysis of thin sections from high-pressure frozen and freeze-substituted specimens revealed a narrow range of SV diameters that peaked at 30 nm at resting synapses (Figure 10A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the figures.

claim: After stimulation and 3 or 10 min recovery, there was a very striking increase in the number of vesicles above 80 nm and a broader distribution of smaller vesicles with a general shift towards larger diameters.
source: After stimulation and 3 or 10 min recovery (Figure 10A,B) not only was there a very striking increase in the number of vesicles above 80 nm (our set point to define vesicles as bulk endosome), but a broader distribution of smaller vesicles with a general shift towards larger diameters was observed.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the figures.

claim: CHC was knocked down in Dyn1/3 DKO neurons by transducing them with lentivirus encoding CHC shRNAmiR.
source: CHC was knocked down in Dyn1/3 DKO neurons by transducing them with lentivirus encoding CHC shRNAmiR or control shRNAmiR. Based on the analysis of GFP co-expressed by the shRNAmiR encoding virus, approximately 90% of the neurons were transduced and massive KD of CHC was confirmed by western blotting (Figure 11A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the figures.

claim: Approximately 90% of the neurons were transduced with lentivirus encoding CHC shRNAmiR.
source: Based on the analysis of GFP co-expressed by the shRNAmiR encoding virus, approximately 90% of the neurons were transduced and massive KD of CHC was confirmed by western blotting (Figure 11A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the figures.

claim: Massive KD of CHC was confirmed by western blotting.
source: Based on the analysis of GFP co-expressed by the shRNAmiR encoding virus, approximately 90% of the neurons were transduced and massive KD of CHC was confirmed by western blotting (Figure 11A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the figures.

claim: A dramatic reduction in CCP abundance in cultures of Dyn1/3 DKO neurons maintained under spontaneous levels of network activity was observed following CHC depletion.
source: As expected, a dramatic reduction in CCP abundance in cultures of Dyn1/3 DKO neurons maintained under spontaneous levels of network activity was observed following CHC depletion (Figure 11B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the figures.

claim: The increase in CCP number produced by the 90 s high K+ stimulation in Dyn1/3 DKO neurons was not observed in cells that had also been depleted of CHC.
source: As expected, the increase in CCP number produced by the 90 s high K+ stimulation in Dyn1/3 DKO neurons was not observed in cells that had also been depleted of CHC (Figure 11D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the figures.

claim: The total recovery of SVs following 30 min of high K+ stimulation was similar at synapses of Dyn1/3 DKO neurons transduced with either the control or CHC KD conditions.
source: However, the total recovery of SVs following 30 min of high K+ stimulation was similar at synapses of Dyn1/3 DKO neurons transduced with either the control or CHC KD conditions (Figure 11C,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the figures.

claim: Stimulation-dependent formation of bulk endosomes and their progressive disappearance during recovery was similar in Dyn1/3 DKO neurons with control or CHC KD.
source: Stimulation-dependent formation of bulk endosomes and their progressive disappearance during recovery was also similar in the two groups of neurons (Figure 11F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the figures.

claim: KD of CHC in Dyn1/3 DKO neurons does not enhance the inhibitory effect on SV recovery when bulk endocytosis is the predominant form of endocytosis.
source: In summary, KD of CHC in Dyn1/3 DKO neurons does not enhance the inhibitory effect on SV recovery when bulk endocytosis is the predominant form of endocytosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study and involves inference about the role of clathrin.

claim: It was proposed that formation of SVs from nerve terminal endosomes could occur via AP-1 and/or AP-3-mediated pathways sensitive to brefeldin A.
source: It was proposed that formation of SVs from nerve terminal endosomes could occur via AP-1 and/or AP-3-mediated pathways sensitive to brefeldin A (Faúndez et al., 1998; Glyvuk et al., 2010; Cheung and Cousin, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Generation of SVs from bulk endosomes during 1 hr recovery still occurred robustly in the presence of brefeldin A (25 μg/ml).
source: However, generation of SVs from bulk endosomes during 1 hr recovery still occurred robustly in the presence of brefeldin A (25 μg/ml) (Figure 12).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the figures.

claim: SV reformation in the presence of latrunculin B (5 μM) argues against an essential role of F-actin.
source: Likewise, SV reformation in the presence of latrunculin B (5 μM) argues against an essential role of F-actin (Figure 12), although actin may be important for bulk endocytosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the figures and involves inference about the role of F-actin.

claim: Actin may be important for bulk endocytosis.
source: Likewise, SV reformation in the presence of latrunculin B (5 μM) argues against an essential role of F-actin (Figure 12), although actin may be important for bulk endocytosis.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential role of actin.

claim: SV reformation following a strong, acute, secretory stimulus occurs predominantly via the budding of SVs from endosomal intermediates generated by bulk endocytosis (bulk endosomes).
source: Our results demonstrate that SV reformation following a strong, acute, secretory stimulus (either high K+ depolarization or high frequency electrical activity) occurs predominantly via the budding of SVs from endosomal intermediates generated by bulk endocytosis (bulk endosomes).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: Formation of bulk endosomes robustly occurs in the absence of dynamin 1 and 3.
source: They show that formation of bulk endosomes robustly occurs in the absence of the two dynamin isoforms (dynamin 1 and 3) that collectively account for the overwhelming majority of neuronal dynamin (Ferguson et al., 2007; Raimondi et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study and citations to prior research.

claim: Dynamin 1 and 3 collectively account for the overwhelming majority of neuronal dynamin.
source: They show that formation of bulk endosomes robustly occurs in the absence of the two dynamin isoforms (dynamin 1 and 3) that collectively account for the overwhelming majority of neuronal dynamin (Ferguson et al., 2007; Raimondi et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Clathrin is not essential for the formation of SVs from bulk endosomes.
source: They further strongly suggest that clathrin is not essential for the formation of SVs from bulk endosomes (Figure 13).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study and involves inference about the role of clathrin.

claim: These data rule out an essential role for the phosphorylation–dephosphorylation cycle of dynamin 1 in bulk endocytosis.
source: By extension, these data rule out an essential role for the phosphorylation–dephosphorylation cycle of dynamin 1 in bulk endocytosis (Anggono et al., 2006; Armbruster et al., 2013), a process that controls the interaction of dynamin 1 with syndapin/pacsin (Anggono et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study and citations to prior research, and involves inference about the role of dynamin 1 phosphorylation.

claim: The phosphorylation–dephosphorylation cycle of dynamin 1 controls the interaction of dynamin 1 with syndapin/pacsin.
source: By extension, these data rule out an essential role for the phosphorylation–dephosphorylation cycle of dynamin 1 in bulk endocytosis (Anggono et al., 2006; Armbruster et al., 2013), a process that controls the interaction of dynamin 1 with syndapin/pacsin (Anggono et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Previous studies had proposed a role of the calcineurin-dependent dephosphorylation of dynamin 1 in bulk endocytosis.
source: This was surprising, as previous studies had proposed a role of the calcineurin-dependent dephosphorylation of dynamin 1 in bulk endocytosis (Clayton et al., 2009, 2010; Xue et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Dynamin 2 could in principle account for the bulk endocytosis occurring in Dyn1/3 DKO cells.
source: Since dynamin 2 is expressed in Dyn1/3 DKO neurons, dynamin 2 could in principle account for the bulk endocytosis occurring in these cells.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential role of dynamin 2.

claim: Dynamin 2 represents only a very minor fraction of total brain dynamin and its levels are not enhanced in Dyn1/3 DKO neurons.
source: However, dynamin 2 represents only a very minor fraction of total brain dynamin and its levels are not enhanced in Dyn1/3 DKO neurons (Raimondi et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The generation of dynamin triple KO synapses has so far proven unfeasible due to the very long half-life of dynamin in axon endings and to the neuronal death that occurs before nerve endings are completely depleted of dynamin 2.
source: While this issue could be solved by the conditional disruption of all the dynamins in neurons, the generation of dynamin triple KO synapses has so far proven unfeasible due to the very long half-life of dynamin in axon endings and to the neuronal death that occurs before nerve endings are completely depleted of dynamin 2 (our unpublished observations).
evidence: This claim is based on unpublished observations by the authors.

claim: The complete KO of all three dynamins was achieved in fibroblasts.
source: The complete KO of all three dynamins was achieved in fibroblasts, as these cells can survive for weeks without any dynamin (Park et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: In triple KO fibroblasts, other forms of endocytosis were not affected, while CME was blocked.
source: Even in triple KO fibroblasts, other forms of endocytosis were not affected, while CME was blocked (Ferguson et al., 2009; Park et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The two neuronal dynamins are specially adapted to support CME during stimulation, and dynamin 2 may account for CME under resting conditions.
source: We suggest that the two neuronal dynamins are specially adapted to support CME during stimulation, and that dynamin 2 may account for CME under resting conditions.
evidence: This is a speculative statement by the authors.

claim: The massive accumulation of clathrin coated pits observed in Dyn1/3 KO cultures slowly disappear upon electrical silencing of the cultures.
source: This would explain why the massive accumulation of clathrin coated pits observed in Dyn1/3 KO cultures slowly disappear upon electrical silencing of the cultures.
evidence: This claim is based on data from the study and involves inference about the role of dynamin 2.

claim: The occurrence of robust SV membrane endocytosis at Dyn1/3 DKO synapses contrasts with the potent global block of the endocytic retrieval of SV membranes in shibirets (dynamin) mutant flies at the restrictive temperature.
source: The occurrence of robust SV membrane endocytosis at Dyn1/3 DKO synapses in spite of the dramatic reduction of dynamin levels also contrasts with the potent global block of the endocytic retrieval of SV membranes in shibirets (dynamin) mutant flies at the restrictive temperature (Kosaka and Ikeda, 1983; Koenig and Ikeda, 1989; Ramaswami et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study and citations to prior research.

claim: Mutant dynamin may produce a potent dominant negative effect by sequestering dynamin interactors.
source: One potential explanation is that mutant dynamin produces a potent dominant negative effect by sequestering dynamin interactors.
evidence: This is a speculative statement by the authors.

claim: The reported strong global blocking effect on SV endocytosis of drugs that impair dynamin action may be explained by the prominent off-target effects of such drugs.
source: Likewise, the reported strong global blocking effect on SV endocytosis of drugs that impair dynamin action (Newton et al., 2006; McCluskey et al., 2013) may be explained by the prominent off-target effects of such drugs (Park et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research and involves speculation about drug effects.

claim: Dynamin 1 is involved in the reformation of SVs that occurs during stimulation.
source: Our results do suggest the involvement of dynamin 1, and by extension its stimulation-dependent dephosphorylation at synapses, in the reformation of SVs that occurs during stimulation, as this process, but not bulk endocytosis, is strikingly abolished by the absence of dynamin 1.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study and involves inference about the role of dynamin 1.

claim: The effect of dynamin 1 absence on SV reformation during stimulation could be explained by a complete block of CME during stimulation.
source: This effect could be explained by a complete block of CME during stimulation, as our studies of dynamin mutant cells have consistently supported a critical role of dynamin in CME (Ferguson et al., 2007, 2009; Hayashi et al., 2008; Raimondi et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study and citations to prior research, and involves speculation about the mechanism.

claim: A block of SV endocytosis was observed at Dyn1 KO and Dyn1/3 DKO synapses during moderate frequency electrical stimulation (300 stimuli at 10 Hz).
source: Since a block of SV endocytosis, as detected by a synaptopHluorin assay (Sankaranarayanan and Ryan, 2001) was observed at Dyn1 KO and Dyn1/3 DKO synapses during moderate frequency electrical stimulation (300 stimuli at 10 Hz), bulk endocytosis was likely not triggered by those experimental conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study and citation to prior research, and involves inference about bulk endocytosis.

claim: The essential role of clathrin in SV reformation was challenged by genetic studies in C. elegans, as synaptic transmission was not abolished in clathrin mutant worms.
source: Concerning clathrin, its essential role in SV reformation (in pathways other than kiss-and-run) was challenged by genetic studies in C. elegans, as synaptic transmission was not abolished in clathrin mutant worms (Sato et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Recent studies of C. elegans and mouse synapses expressing channelrhodopsin and subjected to photostimulation revealed clathrin-independent forms of endocytosis mediated by vacuolar invaginations larger than SVs.
source: Furthermore, recent studies of C. elegans (Kittelmann et al., 2013; Watanabe et al., 2013a) and mouse synapses (Watanabe et al., 2013b) expressing channelrhodopsin and subjected to photostimulation revealed clathrin-independent forms of endocytosis mediated by vacuolar invaginations larger than SVs (Figure 13).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The endocytic reaction described by Kittelmann et al. (2013) following strong photostimulation is reminiscent of the bulk endocytosis described in this study.
source: The endocytic reaction described by Kittelmann et al. (2013) following strong photostimulation is reminiscent of the bulk endocytosis described here.
evidence: This is a statement by the authors comparing their results to prior research.

claim: In the study by Kittelmann et al. (2013), the disappearance of the large vacuoles produced by the intense stimulus was delayed in a dynamints mutant at the restrictive temperature, reminiscent of the delay in the conversion of bulk endosome to SVs observed in Dyn1/3 DKO synapses.
source: Interestingly, in that study the disappearance of the large vacuoles produced by the intense stimulus was delayed in a dynamints mutant at the restrictive temperature, reminiscent of the delay in the conversion of bulk endosome to SVs observed here at Dyn1/3 DKO synapses.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research and comparison to data from the study.

claim: The ultrafast endocytic reaction reported by Watanabe et al. (2013a, 2013b) in either C. elegans or mouse neurons following a very short photostimulus was reported to be dependent on dynamin.
source: In contrast, the ultrafast endocytic reaction reported by Watanabe et al. (2013a, 2013b) in either C. elegans or mouse neurons following a very short photostimulus was reported to be dependent on dynamin, at variance with the endocytic reaction observed in our study.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: SVs are a highly specialized form of small vesicular carriers present in all cells.
source: SVs are a highly specialized form of small vesicular carriers present in all cells.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge.

claim: The prevailing general mechanism for vesicle budding in the secretory and endocytic pathways is the assembly on the donor membrane compartments of a 'coat'.
source: The prevailing general mechanism for vesicle budding in the secretory and endocytic pathways is the assembly on the donor membrane compartments of a 'coat', whose core and accessory subunits are responsible for two major functions: induction of bilayer deformation and protein cargo selection (Faini et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The core and accessory subunits of coats are responsible for induction of bilayer deformation and protein cargo selection.
source: The prevailing general mechanism for vesicle budding in the secretory and endocytic pathways is the assembly on the donor membrane compartments of a 'coat', whose core and accessory subunits are responsible for two major functions: induction of bilayer deformation and protein cargo selection (Faini et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Among the well characterized coats, the only one so far for which there is evidence in SV generation from genetic, biochemical and microscopic observations, is the clathrin coat.
source: Among the well characterized coats, the only one so far for which there is evidence in SV generation from genetic, biochemical and microscopic observations, is the clathrin coat (Heuser and Reese 1973; Maycox et al., 1992; Shupliakov et al., 1997; Nonet et al., 1999; Verstreken et al., 2002; Heerssen et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Clathrin-mediated buds are present only, or at least by far predominantly, on the nerve terminal plasma membrane.
source: However, our study suggests that clathrin-mediated buds are present only, or at least by far predominantly, on the nerve terminal plasma membrane.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: Several membrane-associated scaffolds that mediate budding at the surface of endosomes have been described in recent years.
source: Several membrane-associated scaffolds that mediate budding at the surface of endosomes have been described in recent years (Bonifacino and Rojas, 2006; Schellmann and Pimpl, 2009), but none of them, so far, has been shown to have a critical function in synaptic transmission.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: None of the membrane-associated scaffolds that mediate budding at the surface of endosomes has been shown to have a critical function in synaptic transmission.
source: Several membrane-associated scaffolds that mediate budding at the surface of endosomes have been described in recent years (Bonifacino and Rojas, 2006; Schellmann and Pimpl, 2009), but none of them, so far, has been shown to have a critical function in synaptic transmission.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The membranes of bulk endosomes are expected to be highly enriched in SV proteins, as they form by compensatory endocytosis after SV fusion.
source: The membranes of bulk endosomes are expected to be highly enriched in SV proteins, as they form by compensatory endocytosis after SV fusion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanism of bulk endosome formation.

claim: Protein cargo selection may not be a critical function in the conversion of bulk endosomes to SVs.
source: Thus, protein cargo selection may not be a critical function in this process and mechanisms that force membrane curvature may be sufficient to induce SV formation, albeit perhaps leading to SVs with a non-optimal protein composition and size.
evidence: This is a speculative statement by the authors.

claim: Mechanisms that force membrane curvature may be sufficient to induce SV formation from bulk endosomes, albeit perhaps leading to SVs with a non-optimal protein composition and size.
source: Thus, protein cargo selection may not be a critical function in this process and mechanisms that force membrane curvature may be sufficient to induce SV formation, albeit perhaps leading to SVs with a non-optimal protein composition and size.
evidence: This is a speculative statement by the authors.

claim: Proteins containing BAR domains or other membrane deforming proteins for which there is evidence in SV recycling may be involved in SV formation from bulk endosomes.
source: For example, proteins containing BAR domains (Frost et al., 2009; Campelo et al., 2010) or other membrane deforming proteins for which there is evidence in SV recycling may be involved.
evidence: This is a speculative statement by the authors, supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Direct reformation of SVs from beading and 'imprecise' cutting of tubular structures is a possibility, as supported by the slightly larger and more heterogeneous size of the SVs upon recovery from a massive stimulation.
source: Direct reformation of SVs from beading and 'imprecise' cutting of tubular structures is a possibility, as supported by the slightly larger and more heterogeneous size of the SVs upon recovery from a massive stimulation.
evidence: This is a speculative statement by the authors, supported by data from the study.

claim: Peripheral membrane proteins such as the synapsins may help budding of SVs from bulk endosomes via their bilayer penetrating ALPS motifs.
source: Peripheral membrane proteins such as the synapsins, which are enriched at the surface of SVs (De Camilli et al., 1983), but are shed during the endocytic phase of their recycling, may also help budding of SVs from bulk endosomes via their bilayer penetrating ALPS motifs (Krabben et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a speculative statement by the authors, supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Lipid-mediated mechanisms, that is metabolic changes in the bilayer leading to its spontaneous acquisition of curvature should be considered for SV formation from bulk endosomes.
source: Lipid-mediated mechanisms, that is metabolic changes in the bilayer leading to its spontaneous acquisition of curvature should also be considered.
evidence: This is a speculative statement by the authors.

claim: This mode of SV recycling functions only as a back-up mechanism during intense activity.
source: Importantly, however, we suggest that this mode of SV recycling functions only as a back-up mechanism during intense activity.
evidence: This is a speculative statement by the authors.

claim: At subsequent exo-endocytic cycles, CME may help regenerate SVs with precise size and molecular composition.
source: At subsequent exo-endocytic cycles, CME may help regenerate SVs with precise size and molecular composition.
evidence: This is a speculative statement by the authors.

claim: A direct role for dynamin in the conversion of bulk endosomes to SVs cannot be excluded.
source: A direct role for dynamin in this process cannot be excluded, since in yeast the dynamin homologue Vps1 was implicated in endosomal sorting (Ekena et al., 1993; Chi et al., 2014) and some studies have suggested roles for dynamin on endosomes in mammalian cells (Hayden et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative statement by the authors, supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In yeast the dynamin homologue Vps1 was implicated in endosomal sorting.
source: A direct role for dynamin in this process cannot be excluded, since in yeast the dynamin homologue Vps1 was implicated in endosomal sorting (Ekena et al., 1993; Chi et al., 2014) and some studies have suggested roles for dynamin on endosomes in mammalian cells (Hayden et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Some studies have suggested roles for dynamin on endosomes in mammalian cells.
source: A direct role for dynamin in this process cannot be excluded, since in yeast the dynamin homologue Vps1 was implicated in endosomal sorting (Ekena et al., 1993; Chi et al., 2014) and some studies have suggested roles for dynamin on endosomes in mammalian cells (Hayden et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The conversion of bulk endosomes into SVs still occurs, albeit less efficiently, even in the absence of the two major neuronal dynamin isoforms, pointing to potential dynamin independent mechanisms.
source: However, the conversion of bulk endosomes into SVs still occurs, albeit less efficiently, even in the absence of the two major neuronal dynamin isoforms, pointing to potential dynamin independent mechanisms.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study and involves inference about dynamin-independent mechanisms.

claim: The delay in the conversion from bulk endosomes to SVs observed in Dyn1/3 DKO synapses may be an indirect effect of impaired dynamin function.
source: It is also possible that the delay in the conversion from bulk endosomes to SVs observed in Dyn1/3 DKO synapses may be an indirect effect of impaired dynamin function.
evidence: This is a speculative statement by the authors.

claim: The overload of the bulk endosome to SV conversion pathway in the absence of CME may saturate it.
source: For example, the overload of this pathway in the absence of CME may saturate it.
evidence: This is a speculative statement by the authors.

claim: The absence of dynamin may produce changes in signaling pathways that regulate SV formation from bulk endosomes.
source: Alternatively, the absence of dynamin may produce changes in signaling pathways that regulate SV formation from bulk endosomes. This possibility is supported by the changes that we previously observed in synapsin phosphorylation in Dyn1/3 DKO synapse (Raimondi et al., 2011), which may in turn affect bulk endosome dynamics.
evidence: This is a speculative statement by the authors, supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Changes in synapsin phosphorylation were previously observed in Dyn1/3 DKO synapses, which may in turn affect bulk endosome dynamics.
source: This possibility is supported by the changes that we previously observed in synapsin phosphorylation in Dyn1/3 DKO synapse (Raimondi et al., 2011), which may in turn affect bulk endosome dynamics.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research and involves speculation about the effects on bulk endosome dynamics.

claim: Elucidating the mechanisms underlying the conversion of bulk endosomes into SVs will advance the field of synaptic transmission and provide key new insight in fundamental mechanisms in vesicle biogenesis.
source: Elucidating the mechanisms underlying the conversion of bulk endosomes into SVs will not only advance the field of synaptic transmission but also provide key new insight in fundamental mechanisms in vesicle biogenesis.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential impact of future research.

claim: A paper by Kononenko et al. (2014) reported that bulk endocytosis in response to a strong stimulus is dynamin 1/3 dependent (based on RNA interference) and proposed an important role for clathrin in SV budding from endosomes.
source: While the revision of this manuscript was being finalized, a paper by Kononenko et al. (2014) reported that bulk endocytosis in response to a strong stimulus is dynamin 1/3 dependent (based on RNA interference) and proposed an important role for clathrin in SV budding from endosomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The results of this study, which are based on studies of dynamin 1/3 double KO synapses and on the ultrastructural analysis of the time course of SV recovery from bulk endosomes in the presence or near depletion of clathrin, lead to different conclusions than Kononenko et al. (2014).
source: Our results, which are based on studies of dynamin 1/3 double KO synapses and on the ultrastructrual analysis of the time course of SV recovery from bulk endosomes in the presence or near depletion of clathrin lead to different conclusions.
